0.body: This book specifies the language that interrexx implements: the Rexx language as ooRexx extends it. It describes what a program means, and what the interpreter must do when it runs one.
0.title: Introduction

1.body: The book is written for three readers: an engineer changing the interpreter, who needs the exact behavior before touching code; an LLM agent doing the same work, which may read one page at a time with no history behind it; and a reviewer judging whether a change is correct. It assumes you can read Rexx, and it does not teach the language.
1.title: Who it is for

101.body: A write to a transient stream never seeks. On a FIFO, ooRexx fails a write that follows a still-buffered write, and a close after one, with NOTREADY ERROR:29.
101.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 48. Writing to a transient stream

102.body: A persistent stream keeps separate read and write positions as the reference manual describes, buffered or not: a write starts at the write position, and a relative SEEK moves from the position it names. ooRexx tracks a stale position on a buffered stream, so a write can land on bytes the program never named, and on an unbuffered stream its relative and from-the-end seeks land elsewhere.
102.title: 49. Read and write positions

103.body: When the trace destination refuses a line, the same condition as ooRexx's is raised, but some clauses may do their own work first. ooRexx raises it before the clause does anything.
103.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 50. A trace line that cannot be delivered
103.title: 50. A trace line that cannot be delivered

104.body: Inside an INTERPRET, .context~rs answers the same value as .rs. In ooRexx it answers the caller's earlier value until the INTERPRET ends.
104.title: 51. .context~rs inside INTERPRET

105.body: An output target whose write raises a condition raises 42.3 whatever the command's return code. ooRexx raises it only when the command answers 0.

105.title: 52. An ADDRESS target that fails

106.body: A comparison under NUMERIC FUZZ checks LOSTDIGITS whatever the signs, MAX and MIN apply FUZZ to whole numbers, an omitted MAX or MIN argument is 40.5 for the function and 93.903 for the method, and a divisor is checked for LOSTDIGITS when the dividend is zero. A LOSTDIGITS description renders its operand the same way however it was produced. ooRexx departs from each of these.

106.title: 53. Numeric rules from the reference manual

107.body: CHARS and LINES on a transient stream ask how much input waits and consume none. ooRexx reads a byte to test and loses it, and with /dev/null as standard input its LINES answers 1 where interrexx answers 0.
107.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 54. CHARS and LINES on a transient stream
107.title: 54. CHARS and LINES on a transient stream

108.body: A stream opened WRITE reads nothing: reads fail with ERROR, CHARS and LINES answer 0, and line positioning on a text stream is NOTREADY. ooRexx opens it for reading and writing.
108.title: 55. A stream opened WRITE

109.body: A line position is counted in line ends from the current position, whatever an earlier operation left. ooRexx counts from a line number it tracks, which a character operation resets.
109.title: 56. Line positions

[conv.method] A builtin that runs as a String method does its work by sending the String message of the same name. One of its arguments, usually the first and for a few builtins the second, is the receiver; the others become the message's arguments, in their order. The builtin and the message then give the same result for the same arguments. A builtin page says when its builtin is one of these. The range checks below, and the order of the checks , are rules for these builtins only; any other builtin's page states its own range checks. say substr('abcd', 2, 2) 'abcd'~substr(2, 2) upper('ab', 2) 'ab'~upper(2) bc bc aB aB Note. The ooRexx reference manual (Functions > Built-in Functions) names the builtins that run this way; the ANSI standard, which has no String methods, does not. [conv.position.check] In a builtin that runs as a String method, a position argument is a whole-number argument whose value must be positive. A value of 0 or less raises SYNTAX 93.924; -0 is 0. signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say word('a b', '-0')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say substr('abc', -1)
c: say condition('o')~code 93.924
93.924
93.924 [conv.length.check] In a builtin that runs as a String method, a length argument is a whole-number argument whose value must not be negative. A negative value raises SYNTAX 93.923. A length of 0 is allowed, and so is -0, which is 0. say '['substr('abc', 2, 0)']' '['substr('abc', 2, '-0')']'
signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', 1, -1)
a: say condition('o')~code [] []
93.923 Note. These two codes follow from the reference manual: a builtin of this kind sends a String message, the range of a position or length is checked by that method, and an incorrect call to a method is error 93, whose subcodes 924 and 923 are the position and length cases. The ANSI draft (9.2.1), which has no such methods, raises 40.14 for a position and 40.13 for a length.

112.title: 59. An invalid SEEK

113.body: A '1a'x in a stream is data, at its end too. ooRexx treats a trailing one as end of file when it places writes, and overwrites it.

121.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 68. UNKNOWN of a Stem subclass
121.title: 68. UNKNOWN of a Stem subclass

122.body: The method that evaluates a ::CONSTANT expression is that directive's own, with its own source. ooRexx joins every expression constant of a class into one method, so its source and a run of it differ.
122.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 69. The method of a ::CONSTANT expression
122.title: 69. The method of a ::CONSTANT expression

123.body: DROP, EXPOSE and PROCEDURE EXPOSE process their names and parenthesised lists from left to right. ooRexx processes the parenthesised lists first, in reverse order, then the plain names.
123.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 70. Variable lists run left to right
123.title: 70. Variable lists run left to right

124.body: .context~variables lists a USE ARG alias under the name it is reachable by. ooRexx lists it under the name of the variable it aliases.
124.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 71. A USE ARG alias in .context~variables
124.title: 71. A USE ARG alias in .context~variables

125.body: In every position that requires a string, a variable reference's string value is the referenced value's, and NOSTRING is raised only when that value has none. ooRexx uses the reference's default name and raises NOSTRING for it in most positions.
125.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 72. The string value of a variable reference
125.title: 72. The string value of a variable reference

126.body: A standard descriptor closed when the interpreter starts is open on /dev/null, so writes to it succeed. In ooRexx they fail with ERROR:9.
126.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 73. A standard descriptor closed at start
126.title: 73. A standard descriptor closed at start

127.body: A stream opened APPEND on a file it can only write writes every line at the file's current end. ooRexx writes at the end as it was when opened, overwriting what another writer appended meanwhile.

127.title: 74. APPEND on a write-only file

128.body: While a CALL ON trap is delayed, a condition raised for it again is held as the reference manual describes, and ERROR, FAILURE and NOTREADY raised again are ignored. ooRexx loses a held condition raised from a routine the handler calls, and crashes in some such programs.
128.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 75. A condition raised while its CALL trap is delayed
128.title: 75. A condition raised while its CALL trap is delayed

[conv.arg.omitted] An argument is omitted when its place in the argument list holds no expression: nothing before the first comma, nothing between two commas, or nothing after the last one. An omitted optional argument takes the default that its page states. say substr('abc', 1, , '.') substr('abc', 2, ) abc bc [conv.arg.empty] An argument whose expression yields the null string is not omitted and never takes the default. It is checked like any other value: as a whole number it raises SYNTAX 40.12 ( whole-number form ), as a pad SYNTAX 40.23 ( pad ), and as a string it is the null string. signal on syntax name a

a: say condition('o')~code

130.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 77. The string value of a stem

132.body: On a stream opened APPEND, the write position cannot be moved into the file as it was when opened: such a SEEK answers 0, and a CHAROUT or LINEOUT naming a position there writes nothing, all NOTREADY. ooRexx moves the position, and a LINEOUT naming a line writes there.

133.body: The first SEEK of a transient stream that nothing has opened raises 93.958, as any positioning of a transient stream does. ooRexx answers 1.
133.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 80. First SEEK of an unopened transient stream
133.title: 80. First SEEK of an unopened transient stream

134.body: A stem's STRING sends STRING to its default value. ooRexx answers the default's default name. A trace value line still shows the default's name.
134.title: 81. A stem's STRING method

135.body: A LINEOUT that closes a FIFO consumes no input. ooRexx consumes a byte.
135.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 82. Closing LINEOUT on a FIFO
135.title: 82. Closing LINEOUT on a FIFO

136.title: 83. When RAISE DESCRIPTION is converted

138.title: 85. .environment per interpreter

139.body: The rxapi daemon starts only when a program first needs it, and prints its own messages. ooRexx starts it with every interpreter.

[conv.check.order] In a builtin that runs as a String method, when more than one argument fails, the form checks run first: the whole-number checks of form and value , and the pad check, applied to the arguments from left to right, and the first failure is raised. Only when every argument passes them do the range checks of positions and lengths run, again from left to right. A builtin page that has checks of its own states where they fall in this order. signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', 0, 'x')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say substr('abc', 0, 1, '**')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say substr('abc', 'x', 1, '**')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say translate('abc', , , '**', 'x')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say substr('abc', 0, -1)
f: say condition('o')~code 40.12

The reference manual does not say that the function call checks the form of its arguments, under error 40, before it sends the message; that part matches ooRexx. The ANSI draft (9.2.1) checks each argument's form and range together, one argument at a time.

144.title: 91. A command whose child was already reaped

[conv.error.name] A rule that says something "raises SYNTAX m.n" means that the builtin returns no value and the SYNTAX condition is raised with error number m and subcode n. A trap for it sees condition('C') as SYNTAX, condition('O')~code as the string m.n, and the variable RC set to m. This book does not state the error message. signal on syntax name e
x = substr('abc', 0)
say 'not reached'
e: say condition('c') condition('o')~code rc SYNTAX 93.924 93 [conv.returns] A rule that says a builtin "returns" a string means that the function call's value is exactly that string: the same characters in the same order, with no blanks added or removed. say '['substr('abc', 2)']' '['substr(' a ', 1)']' [bc] [ a ]

16.body:
[conv.string.deviation.30] interrexx does not convert an argument whose STRING method answers an object that is not a string, such as a Directory. When a builtin receives such an argument where its page calls for a string, interrexx ends the program with exit code 120 and a message that this is not implemented, after raising NOSTRING when a trap for it is set. ooRexx reads the answer as a string, and what it does then depends on the builtin: UPPER ends the program with Error 5, LENGTH answers an unrelated number, and STRIP crashes the interpreter. A program can rely on none of these answers. o = .weird~new
say 'before'
say upper(o)
say 'after'
::class weird
::method string return .directory~new before

A name in square brackets is an optional argument; every other argument is required. 18.body:
[bif.index.words.split] The builtins that count words split a string into words the same way. A word is a run of one or more characters, none of them whitespace , that has whitespace or an end of the string on each side. The words of a string are numbered from 1, left to right. Whitespace before the first word, between two words and after the last belongs to no word, so the null string and a string of only whitespace have no words. Every other character, line feed and '00'x among them, can be part of a word. say words(' a'||'09'x||'b c ') words('') words(' '||'09'x)
say word('one two', 2) c2x(word('a'||'0a000c'x||'b c', 1)) 3 0 0
two 610A000C62 Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.26 and the other word builtins) separates words by a set of blank characters that it leaves to the configuration: the blank and any others the configuration names. ooRexx fixes that set as the blank and the horizontal tab, and so does this book. [bif.index.words.number] Where a word builtin's page calls an argument a word number, that argument is a position that counts words: the word number n names word n of the string as the word rule numbers them. A word number greater than the number of words in the string is not an error, for every value that passes its check; it names no word, and the builtin's page says what the builtin answers then. say '['word('a b', 3)']' wordindex('a b', 3) wordlength('a b', 999999999999999999), wordpos('a', 'a b', 3)
signal on syntax name e
say wordindex('a b', 0)
e: say condition('o')~code [] 0 0 0

2.body: This book is normative in its own right: its rules define the language interrexx implements, and no other document or implementation does. When the interpreter and a rule disagree, one of them has a defect, and the disagreement is settled here before it is settled in code. Behavior the book does not state is not promised, and where a reader might expect a promise the book says explicitly that a behavior is not specified. Rules and examples are normative. 3.body: ooRexx. The open-source C++ implementation of Object Rexx, version 5. interrexx is written to run ooRexx programs, and the book's examples are also run on ooRexx to measure where the two agree. Deviation. A declared difference between interrexx and ooRexx, numbered in the Deviations chapter . A page lists in its front matter the deviations that touch its element, and states each as a rule whose identifier ends deviation.N. Every example on which interrexx and ooRexx answer differently belongs to such a rule; any other difference is a defect. String method. A method of the String class. Many builtins run as one, as the conventions define. Identity. Whether two values are the same object, as opposed to equal strings. It is observable only through identityHash and the identity collections (IdentityTable, IdentitySet), and the book says where it is not specified.

4.body: Every statement the book makes about behavior is a rule. A rule has an identifier of dotted lowercase words, and it is a single short paragraph. An identifier names the page that holds its rule, so a reader of the raw Markdown finds any rule from its identifier alone. The first word names the chapter: bif for built-in functions in builtins/, instr for instructions/, expr for expressions/, parse for parsing/, cond for conditions/ and class for classes/. The second word is the page's file name: bif.substr.pad is in builtins/substr.md, and the rules for a whole chapter, such as bif.index.call.count, are in its index.md. The conventions are one page, conventions.md, and every conv. rule is there. The checker rejects a rule on any other page. Identifiers never change and are never reused. Other pages refer to a rule by that identifier, and so do comments in the test sources: a test that exercises a rule cites it, and the checker reports any rule that has neither a cited test nor an example.

52.body: A Deviation is a declared difference between interrexx and ooRexx. Every example on which the two answer differently belongs to one; any other difference is a defect.
